intro: This is the classic winter question: keep the whole-house heat pump doing its job, or shut the bedroom door and run a space heater? The physics differ completely — a space heater converts electricity to heat 1:1, while a heat pump moves 2–4 units of heat per unit of electricity.
verdict: Per unit of heat delivered, the heat pump wins by a wide margin — typically 2–4× cheaper. The space heater only wins when it lets you heat one small room while the heat pump (and the rest of the house) stays turned way down. Heating multiple rooms with space heaters is the most expensive common heating mistake in America.

intro: Both solve 'I'm cold at night' — one by heating the room, the other by heating the bed. The wattage gap is enormous: 1,500 watts versus about 150.
verdict: The electric blanket costs roughly a tenth as much for sleeping comfort and is the clear winner at night. The space heater only makes sense when you need the whole room warm — working at a desk, kids playing on the floor. For sleeping, blanket first, heater only if pipes or comfort truly demand a warm room.

intro: An electric fireplace is marketed as ambiance plus heat; a space heater is pure function. Under the shell they are the same device — a resistance element and a fan.
verdict: It's a tie on heating cost: both deliver ~1,500 watts of resistance heat at identical price per hour. The fireplace's flame effect alone costs almost nothing, so run visuals without heat freely. Buy whichever you'll enjoy — just don't expect the fireplace to heat more cheaply.

intro: Fan heaters blast warm air immediately; oil-filled radiators warm slowly and coast after shutoff. People often assume the 'gentler' radiator is cheaper.
verdict: Identical cost per hour at the same wattage — resistance heat is resistance heat. The radiator's thermal mass can save a little via thermostat cycling and comfort at lower settings, while the fan heater wins for quick bursts in small spaces. Pick by noise and use pattern, not efficiency claims.

intro: Infrared heaters claim to 'heat objects, not air,' and marketing often implies dramatic savings over conventional space heaters.
verdict: Watt for watt, cost is identical. Infrared's real advantage is targeting: in a garage or drafty room, radiant heat can make you comfortable without warming all the air, effectively letting you run fewer watts. In a sealed small room, there's no meaningful difference. Ignore '50% savings' marketing.

intro: Homes with electric baseboards often wonder if plug-in space heaters would be cheaper. Both are resistance heat, so the per-kWh price of warmth is the same — the difference is control.
verdict: A draw on raw rates, but space heaters often win in practice because you place them where you are and switch them off when you leave, while baseboards heat whole rooms on wall thermostats. Best answer: keep baseboards low for baseline, spot-heat occupied rooms carefully. Never run a space heater unattended or overnight.

intro: This is the biggest heating-bill decision in all-electric homes: resistance furnace strips versus a modern heat pump compressor.
verdict: The heat pump wins decisively — typically half to a third the cost for the same warmth in most U.S. climates, and modern cold-climate units hold their advantage well below freezing. The furnace only 'wins' as backup during extreme cold or defrost. If you heat with an electric furnace today, a heat pump is usually the single highest-return upgrade available.

intro: Conventional dryers heat air and throw it out a vent; heat pump dryers recycle it. The efficiency gap is the largest of any common appliance pair.
verdict: The heat pump dryer uses roughly 40–60% less energy per load and wins clearly on running cost — the higher purchase price typically pays back in a few years for families drying several loads weekly, faster in high-rate states. Conventional wins only on cycle speed and upfront price.

intro: Both dry clothes with heat; one buys that heat as electricity, the other as natural gas. The electric meter tells only part of the story.
verdict: On energy cost per load, gas usually wins — often by half — because gas heat is cheaper per BTU in most states. Electric wins where gas service doesn't exist or rates are unusually low. If you already have a gas hookup in the laundry, a gas dryer is typically the cheaper decade-long choice.

intro: Cooling the whole house versus cooling the room you're in — the most consequential summer cost decision for many households.
verdict: For one or two occupied rooms, window units win by a large margin: cooling 300 square feet simply takes far less energy than 2,000. Central wins on comfort, humidity control, and whole-family use. The cheapest strategy for many homes is central AC set warmer, with a window unit handling the one room that needs to be truly cold.

intro: Ducted central AC versus ductless mini-splits is both a comfort and an efficiency decision — and duct losses are the hidden variable.
verdict: Mini-splits generally win on cost: no duct losses (which waste 20–30% in typical attics), inverter compressors that sip at part load, and per-room zoning. Central wins on whole-house evenness and existing infrastructure. For additions, bonus rooms, or replacing window units, the mini-split is the efficiency choice.

intro: They cost about the same to buy and claim similar BTUs, but window and portable ACs are not equals on the bill.
verdict: The window unit wins clearly. Single-hose portables exhaust indoor air outside, pulling warm air in through every gap — much of each kilowatt-hour fights itself. Expect a portable to cost 30–70% more for the same actual cooling. Choose portable only when a window mount is truly impossible; dual-hose models close part of the gap.

intro: The premium room-cooling option versus the budget classic: an inverter mini-split against a window unit.
verdict: The mini-split typically cools the same room for one-third to one-half the electricity, runs quieter, and heats in winter too. The window unit wins on upfront cost by a factor of five or more. High electricity rates and year-round use favor the mini-split's payback; occasional summer use in a cheap-power state favors the window unit.

intro: A fan moves air; an air conditioner refrigerates it. They're often framed as rivals, but they solve different problems at wildly different wattages.
verdict: The fan costs 5–10% as much per hour and wins whenever moving air is enough — which is more often than most people think, since a breeze makes a room feel several degrees cooler. The AC wins when humidity or real heat make air movement insufficient. The smart play is both: AC set warmer, fan making it feel cooler.

intro: The full-size oven versus the countertop convection basket — a question practically invented by the last five years of kitchens.
verdict: For anything that fits in the basket, the air fryer wins: less mass to heat, no preheat, shorter cook times — typically half the energy or better. The oven wins for volume cooking, where one big batch beats three air-fryer rounds. In summer, the air fryer wins twice by not heating the kitchen your AC is cooling.

intro: Same job, different cavity size — and cavity size is most of what an oven's energy bill is.
verdict: The toaster oven wins for small dishes, using one-third to one-half the energy. The crossover comes with quantity: once you're cooking for a family or using multiple racks, the big oven's single session beats repeated small ones. Rule of thumb: if it fits comfortably in the toaster oven, that's the cheaper appliance.

intro: Eight hours at 200 watts versus one hour at 2,400 — the tortoise-and-hare of kitchen energy.
verdict: Roughly a tie on energy per meal, with the slow cooker usually edging ahead — its long runtime at low wattage totals about the same or slightly less than an hour of oven cycling. The slow cooker wins decisively in summer by not heating the kitchen, and on cheap cuts it wins the grocery bill too.

intro: For reheating and small portions, the microwave and the stovetop burner compete daily in every kitchen.
verdict: The microwave wins for reheating, typically using half to a quarter of the energy — it heats food directly instead of a pan and the air around it. The stove wins on results for anything needing browning, crisping, or precise control. For leftovers and vegetables, microwave first is the frugal default.

intro: Boiling water is the most-repeated cooking task in most homes, and the two common tools differ more than people expect.
verdict: The electric kettle wins — it transfers nearly all its energy directly into the water and shuts off at the boil, beating an open pot on a radiant burner by 30–50%. Induction cooktops narrow the gap but don't close it. Boil only the water you need and the kettle's win doubles.

intro: Both run on electricity; only one turns most of it into heat inside the pan.
verdict: Induction wins: roughly 85–90% of energy reaches the food versus ~70–75% for radiant coils, and its speed reduces total cooking minutes. The savings are modest in dollars — cooking isn't a huge bill line — but induction also wins on control, safety, and summer kitchen heat. Radiant's only win is upfront price and no cookware requirements.

intro: Hot water is typically the second-largest energy use in an all-electric home, which makes this comparison worth real money.
verdict: The heat pump water heater wins overwhelmingly — the same showers on roughly one-third the electricity, often saving $200–500 per year depending on state rates and household size. Resistance tanks win only on upfront cost and in unheated spaces too cold for a heat pump to work well. With current federal and utility incentives, payback is often under three years.

intro: Storage tank versus on-demand: the tank keeps 50 gallons hot all day; tankless heats ferociously only while a tap runs.
verdict: Tankless wins modestly on energy — eliminating standby losses typically saves 10–25% — but electric tankless demands enormous instantaneous power that may require panel upgrades. The tank wins on install cost and off-peak flexibility. If the goal is purely a lower bill, a heat pump water heater beats both.

intro: Surely the little fridge costs less than the big one? Per cubic foot, the answer flips.
verdict: The full-size refrigerator is far more efficient per unit of storage — a modern 20 cu ft unit often uses only 1.5–2× the energy of a 3 cu ft mini. As a second fridge for a few drinks, the mini wins on absolute draw; but consolidating everything into one efficient full-size unit and unplugging the mini is the cheapest configuration of all.

intro: Same capacity, different door orientation — and cold air behaves very differently in each.
verdict: The chest freezer wins on running cost by 20–40%: cold air stays pooled inside when the lid opens, seals are simpler, and most models skip energy-hungry auto-defrost. The upright wins on organization and floor space. If it lives in a hot garage, the chest freezer's advantage grows.

intro: A high-end gaming PC and a PS5 or Series X render similar games with very different silicon budgets.
verdict: The console wins on electricity, drawing 150–220 watts against a serious PC's 300–800. Over four hours a night, that gap is real but modest in dollars — a few dollars a month in most states. The PC's flexibility fairly costs a premium; capping frame rates claws much of it back.

intro: For everyday computing, the desktop-versus-laptop choice is quietly also an energy choice.
verdict: The laptop wins by 3–5×, doing the same browsing and office work on 30–60 watts versus 150–250 for a desktop and monitor. Full-time laptop use saves a modest but real amount every year. The desktop wins only when you actually need its sustained performance — and even then, sleep settings matter more than the hardware.

intro: The most settled matchup in home energy, still worth quantifying because the numbers are so lopsided.
verdict: LED wins by roughly 85% per bulb — 9 watts doing the work of 60 — and lasts 15–25× longer. A whole-house conversion typically pays for itself within months. There is no scenario in which buying new incandescents makes financial sense; the only question left is how quickly you replace the survivors.

intro: Low and slow versus hot and fast: two paths to the same braise, hours apart.
verdict: The electric pressure cooker usually wins on energy — intense heating for a short time beats gentle heating for eight hours, typically by 30–50% per meal. The slow cooker wins on set-and-forget convenience and gentler textures. Both beat the oven; either is a frugal choice, so pick by cooking style.
